name: MMseqs2
compares: Amino-acid letters: it first keeps target proteins that share similar short words with the query, then aligns only those, which makes it much faster than aligning every pair.
reference: The relative's proteome (Quest for Orthologs reference proteomes, release 2020_04), as an MMseqs2 database.
score: Bit score: higher ranks first. The E-value cutoff was 10.
failure_modes: At most 1,000 target proteins are kept per query (--max-seqs 1000), so a query from a very large family can lose hits. How often: not measured.
command:
mmseqs search \
    human-38fdd87d_mmdb/db zebrafish_mmdb/db result mmseqs_tmp \
    --threads 16 \
    -s 7 \
    --max-seqs 1000 \
    -e 10.0

cost_per_1000_queries.hardware: Stanford Sherlock, SLURM partition hns; searches on CPU only

questions: Is the closest same-family domain in the relative you will search at least 40% identical, for most of your proteins? If yes, Fmax here is 40–60% 0.249 (n = 563), 60–100% 0.297 (n = 1,289). If no, 20–30% 0.325 (n = 93), 30–40% 0.188 (n = 165). (Pfam truth set, raw calls, zebrafish (430 Mya) as the relative searched, setting `s7`; strata with at least 30 true instances.)

Are the features you care about longer than 60 residues? If yes, Fmax here is 61–120 aa 0.243 (n = 963), 121–250 aa 0.305 (n = 504), 251 aa or more 0.462 (n = 277). If no, 16–30 aa 0.027 (n = 271), 31–60 aa 0.089 (n = 420). (Pfam truth set, raw calls, zebrafish (430 Mya) as the relative searched, setting `s7`.)
Can you spend about 0.0194 CPU-hours per 1,000 proteins for each relative you search? That is the measured cost against zebrafish; the range over relatives is under "Cost per 1,000 queries" above.
